What is the primary function of an operating system?
The primary function of an operating system is to manage hardware resources and provide services for computer programs.
Who is credited with creating the first operating system?
General Motors and North American Aviation are credited with creating the first operating system for the IBM 704 in 1956.
What was the name of the first widely used operating system for personal computers?
CP/M (Control Program for Microcomputers) was the first widely used operating system for personal computers in the late 1970s.
Which operating system introduced the graphical user interface to a mass audience?
Apple's Macintosh operating system, introduced in 1984, brought the graphical user interface to a mass audience.
UNICS (Uniplexed Information and Computing Service) was the original name, later shortened to UNIX.
Who developed the UNIX operating system?
Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, and others at Bell Labs developed UNIX in 1969.
What programming language was used to rewrite UNIX in 1973, making it portable?
The C programming language was used to rewrite UNIX in 1973, enabling portability across hardware.
What is the relationship between Linux and UNIX?
Linux is a Unix-like operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991, inspired by UNIX but not derived from its code.
What was the first version of Microsoft Windows released in 1985?
Windows 1.0 was the first version of Microsoft Windows, released in November 1985.
Which operating system was dominant in the 1990s for business and home PCs?
Microsoft Windows, particularly Windows 95 and Windows 98, dominated the PC market in the 1990s.
What is the kernel in an operating system?
The kernel is the core component of an operating system that manages system resources and communication between hardware and software.
What is the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
A monolithic kernel runs all operating system services in kernel space, while a microkernel runs only essential services in kernel space and moves others to user space.
Which operating system uses the X Window System as its graphical foundation?
Many Unix-like operating systems, including Linux distributions, use the X Window System as the foundation for their graphical user interfaces.
What is the purpose of a shell in an operating system?
A shell provides a user interface for interacting with the operating system, typically through command-line input.
What does POSIX stand for and what is its purpose?
POSIX stands for Portable Operating System Interface and defines standards to ensure compatibility between Unix-like operating systems.
What was the significance of the release of Windows NT 3.1 in 1993?
Windows NT 3.1 was the first fully 32-bit, portable, and secure version of Windows designed for business and enterprise use.
What operating system powers the majority of web servers today?
Linux-based operating systems power the majority of web servers today due to their stability, security, and open-source nature.
What is the name of the operating system used in Apple's Macintosh computers since 2001?
macOS is the operating system used in Apple's Macintosh computers since 2001, succeeding Mac OS X.
What is the relationship between iOS and macOS?
iOS and macOS share a common Unix-based foundation (Darwin) and many frameworks, but are tailored for different device types.
What was the first operating system to support preemptive multitasking on a personal computer?
AmigaOS, released in 1985, was one of the first operating systems to support preemptive multitasking on a personal computer.
What does the term 'open source' mean in the context of operating systems?
Open source means the source code of the operating system is freely available for anyone to view, modify, and distribute.
Which operating system was developed as a free alternative to MINIX?
Linux was developed by Linus Torvalds as a free alternative to MINIX, a Unix-like system used for teaching.
What is the role of device drivers in an operating system?
Device drivers are software components that allow the operating system to communicate with and control hardware devices.
What is virtual memory in an operating system?
Virtual memory is a memory management technique that gives an application the impression it has contiguous working memory, using disk space to extend physical RAM.
What is the purpose of a file system in an operating system?
A file system organizes and manages how data is stored, retrieved, and updated on storage devices.
Which operating system introduced the concept of plug and play hardware detection?
Windows 95 introduced plug and play functionality, allowing the operating system to automatically detect and configure hardware.
What is the name of the operating system used in Google's Android smartphones?
Android is based on the Linux kernel and uses a modified version of it as its core operating system.
What was the significance of the release of Solaris by Sun Microsystems?
Solaris was a Unix-based operating system known for its scalability, reliability, and advanced features in enterprise environments.
What does the acronym DOS stand for in the context of early PCs?
DOS stands for Disk Operating System, referring to systems like MS-DOS that managed disk storage and program execution.
Which operating system was the first to include networking as a core feature?
UNIX was among the first operating systems to include networking capabilities as a fundamental part of its design.
What is the difference between a process and a thread in an operating system?
A process is an independent program with its own memory space, while a thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares memory and resources.
What operating system is used in the majority of supercomputers today?
Linux-based operating systems are used in the majority of the world's fastest supercomputers.
What is the purpose of a bootloader in an operating system?
A bootloader is a small program that loads the operating system kernel into memory when a computer starts up.
What is the name of the operating system developed by IBM for its mainframe systems?
IBM developed z/OS, a 64-bit operating system for its mainframe computers.
What is the significance of the release of Mac OS X in 2001?
Mac OS X introduced a Unix-based foundation (Darwin) to Apple's Macintosh line, improving stability, security, and performance.
What is the role of interrupts in an operating system?
Interrupts are signals that temporarily halt the CPU's current task to handle urgent events, allowing the operating system to manage hardware and software efficiently.
What is the name of the open-source operating system derived from Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD)?
FreeBSD, OpenBSD, and NetBSD are open-source operating systems derived from the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD).
What is the purpose of a system call in an operating system?
A system call allows a user-level program to request a service from the operating system's kernel, such as reading a file or allocating memory.
What operating system was used on the Apollo Guidance Computer?
The Apollo Guidance Computer used a real-time operating system developed by MIT, not a commercial OS like UNIX or Windows.
What is the significance of the release of Windows XP in 2001?
Windows XP combined the consumer-friendly interface of Windows 98 with the stability and security of the Windows NT kernel, becoming one of the most widely used operating systems in history.

What is the difference between the Internet and the World Wide Web?
The Internet is a global network of interconnected computers, while the World Wide Web is a system of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via the Internet using web browsers.
Who invented the World Wide Web?
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN.
HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
What is the purpose of a URL?
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) specifies the address of a resource on the web and how to retrieve it.
What protocol is used to send and receive email?
Email is typically sent and received using the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) for sending and IMAP or POP3 for receiving.
An IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to each device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication.
What does DNS stand for and what does it do?
DNS stands for Domain Name System and translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
A web browser is a software application used to retrieve, render, and display content from the World Wide Web.
HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) is used to structure and present content on web pages.
What is the function of a router in a home network?
A router directs data packets between devices on a local network and between the local network and the Internet.
What is HTTPS and why is it more secure than HTTP?
HTTPS is HTTP secured with TLS/SSL encryption, protecting data transmitted between a user's browser and a website from interception or tampering.
What is a cookie in web browsing?
A cookie is a small piece of data stored on a user's device by a website to remember information about the user, such as login status or preferences.
ISP stands for Internet Service Provider, a company that provides individuals and organizations access to the Internet.
What is bandwidth in the context of internet connections?
Bandwidth refers to the maximum rate of data transfer across a network connection, typically measured in bits per second.
A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules.
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services—including servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and analytics—over the Internet.
A search engine is a web-based tool that indexes and retrieves information from the web in response to user queries.
What is the purpose of the 'www' in a web address?
The 'www' subdomain traditionally indicates that a host is part of the World Wide Web, though it is not technically required.
Phishing is a fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information by disguising as a trustworthy entity in electronic communication.
Two-factor authentication is a security process requiring two different forms of verification to access an account, such as a password and a code from a mobile device.
What is a VPN and what does it do?
A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates a secure, encrypted connection over a less secure network, such as the Internet, to protect privacy and bypass geographic restrictions.
Net neutrality is the principle that Internet service providers should treat all data on the Internet equally, without discriminating or charging differently by user, content, website, or platform.
What is a server in the context of the web?
A server is a computer or system that provides resources, data, services, or programs to other computers, known as clients, over a network.
What is JavaScript used for on websites?
JavaScript is a programming language used to add interactivity, dynamic content, and client-side functionality to web pages.
A domain name is a human-readable address used to identify a website on the Internet, such as example.com.
What is the role of a web host?
A web host provides the technologies and services needed for a website to be viewed on the Internet, including server space and connectivity.
AJAX (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML) is a technique used to update parts of a web page without reloading the entire page.
Responsive web design is an approach to web development that ensures web pages render well on a variety of devices and window or screen sizes.
What is the purpose of the 'robots.txt' file?
The robots.txt file instructs web crawlers which pages or sections of a website should not be accessed or indexed.
A 404 error is an HTTP status code indicating that the server could not find the requested resource.
What is the difference between GET and POST HTTP methods?
GET retrieves data from a server and appends parameters to the URL, while POST sends data to a server in the request body, typically for submitting forms.
A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a geographically distributed network of servers that delivers web content to users based on their geographic location to improve loading speed and reliability.
What is the function of a modem?
A modem modulates and demodulates signals to enable digital data to be transmitted over analog communication channels, such as telephone or cable lines.
What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?
The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to the network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity to exchange data over the Internet.
Open source software is software whose source code is made available for anyone to inspect, modify, and enhance.
What is the purpose of SSL/TLS certificates?
SSL/TLS certificates authenticate the identity of a website and enable encrypted communication between the web server and the browser.
A web API (Application Programming Interface) allows different software applications to communicate with each other over the Internet using standard protocols like HTTP.
What is the difference between a static and a dynamic web page?
A static web page displays the same content to every user, while a dynamic web page generates content in real time based on user input, database queries, or other variables.
What is the role of CSS in web design?
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is used to control the presentation, layout, and visual appearance of web pages written in HTML or XML.
What is the significance of port 80 and port 443?
Port 80 is the default port for HTTP traffic, and port 443 is the default port for HTTPS traffic.
A proxy server acts as an intermediary between a user's device and the Internet, forwarding requests and responses while potentially providing caching, filtering, or anonymity.
What is the purpose of the 'alt' attribute in an HTML image tag?
The 'alt' attribute provides alternative text for an image, which is displayed if the image cannot be loaded and is important for accessibility and SEO.
What is the difference between intranet and extranet?
An intranet is a private network accessible only to an organization's members, while an extranet extends intranet access to authorized external users such as partners or clients.

Henry Ford founded Ford Motor Company in 1903.

BMW was founded in 1916 as Bayerische Flugzeugwerke AG, later renamed Bayerische Motoren Werke (BMW) in 1922; its origins trace to Karl Rapp and Gustav Otto.

Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia, and Nathan Blecharczyk founded Airbnb in 2008.
Tobias Lütke, Daniel Weinand, and Scott Lake founded Shopify in 2006.
Eric Yuan founded Zoom Video Communications in 2011.
Marc Benioff, Parker Harris, Dave Moellenhoff, and Frank Dominguez founded Salesforce in 1999.
Michael Dell founded Dell Technologies in 1984.

William E. Boeing founded Boeing in 1916.
Who founded The New York Times?
Henry Jarvis Raymond and George Jones founded The New York Times in 1851.
Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger co-founded Wikipedia in 2001.
